summary: Describes use cases for managing networks that contain constrained devices. It is the companion to RFC 7547, which gives the problem statement and requirements, and gives concrete scenarios that motivate them.

plainLanguage.summary: Real-life stories of tiny connected gadgets and how someone might need to look after them. They show why the requirements in the companion document are needed.

subtitle: Real-world scenarios for managing networks of resource-limited devices.

tldr.problem: Networks containing constrained devices (limited power, memory, and processing) present management challenges different from traditional IP networks, and diverse application scenarios need different approaches.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs ten detailed use cases—from environmental monitoring to medical devices to industrial automation—showing what management systems need to handle and how responsibility transfers across the device lifecycle.
tldr.outcome: The requirements derived from these scenarios drive the design of management protocols and systems that work with IoT, sensor networks, and embedded devices in the field.

facts.label: Use cases described
facts.value: 10: from environmental monitoring to field operations

facts.label: Access technologies
facts.value: IEEE 802.15.4, Bluetooth Low Energy, DECT ULE, cellular gateways

today: RFC 7548 is Informational and describes the motivating scenarios for the companion RFC 7547 (problem statement and requirements). These use cases guide the design of management protocols and systems for networks with constrained devices.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Constrained devices—also called sensors, smart objects, or smart devices—are computers with limited CPU, memory, and power. They are increasingly deployed in networks where they monitor conditions, control equipment, or both. These devices may operate alone or in groups, sometimes via a gateway that translates to the wider internet, sometimes directly on unconstrained networks.

Managing networks that include constrained devices differs from managing traditional IP networks. Constrained devices have limited power (often battery-powered), may be unreliable (lossy wireless links), operate in harsh environments (natural ecosystems, factories, underwater), and may need to work unsupervised for long periods. Traditional network management—periodically collecting data from devices, processing it, and displaying results—must adapt to these constraints.

The RFC describes use cases across industries and device types, showing what challenges managers face and how management responsibility shifts across a device's lifetime (manufacturing, installation, operation, replacement, decommissioning).
sections.plainLanguage: Millions of tiny, battery-powered sensors and devices are now connected to networks, measuring temperature, controlling valves, and reporting data. Unlike computers on an office network, these devices are hard to reach, go weeks without charging, and are deployed in places like fields and factories. Managing them requires different tools and approaches.

sections.title: Access Technologies and Device Lifecycles
sections.content:
Constrained devices use low-power, low-bandwidth wireless technologies such as IEEE 802.15.4, Bluetooth Low Energy, or DECT Ultra Low Energy to communicate. These technologies have small frame sizes, so management protocols and messages must be carefully designed to avoid packet fragmentation, which consumes precious memory on resource-limited devices.

Cellular gateways—smartphones, femtocells, or embedded LTE modules—can also connect constrained devices to networks. In such scenarios, a gateway device may manage the constrained devices connected to it, while a network management system (NMS) communicates only with the gateway. This hierarchical approach reduces the management load on constrained devices themselves.

Device management passes through distinct phases. During manufacturing and testing, the device maker is responsible and performs quality assurance. During installation and configuration, management responsibility transfers to an installer (who may be the customer or a contractor). During operation and maintenance, the customer or a contracted maintenance provider takes over. During replacement or decommissioning, the manager ensures proper handoff, data removal, or destruction. At each phase, the NMS must support transferring responsibility and managing access permissions.
sections.plainLanguage: Sensors use weak wireless links and can only handle tiny messages. Sometimes they talk through a hub device that then connects to the main network. As a device moves from the factory to a home or building, different people (makers, installers, customers, repair services) take responsibility for managing it.

sections.title: Environmental and Infrastructure Monitoring
sections.content:
Environmental monitoring deploys sensors across wide geographic areas to track emissions, water quality, wildlife, earthquakes, or tsunamis. Sensors are often mobile, difficult to replace, and exposed to tampering.

Infrastructure monitoring tracks bridges, railway tracks, windmills, and similar structures for safety. A network combines fixed and wireless technologies, may be widely distributed, and often uses more capable devices than basic sensors. Both types of monitoring must tolerate failures gracefully (repairs may take days or cost more than replacement) and protect data from tampering in safety-critical scenarios.

Industrial applications—including smart manufacturing, asset tracking, process control, and optimization—require networks to deliver sensor data to control systems in real time, sometimes in seconds. Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) for Condition-Based Maintenance let operators monitor inaccessible or moving machinery. Management must ensure continuous monitoring, handle rapid responses, provide multi-level access control, and support both local diagnostics and remote monitoring from outside the factory.
sections.plainLanguage: Farms and nature reserves use sensors spread across huge areas to watch for floods or pollution. Factories use sensors on machines to predict when they will break before they actually do, so operators can fix them in time. Bridges have sensors watching for cracks. All of these networks must keep working even when some sensors fail, and must protect important information from hackers.

sections.title: Energy, Medical, and Home Applications
sections.content:
Energy management applies to the smart grid, where utilities monitor and control power distribution and consumption. Smart metering reads electric usage from many meters and aggregates the data. Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) networks connect utilities to meters at homes and businesses, often through mesh networks with low-bandwidth radios. Unlike simple meters, AMI systems must manage thousands of nodes organized ad hoc, work over multiple management domains (meters may be on poles owned by separate entities), and robustly perform firmware updates without disrupting critical power systems.

Medical applications range from wearable monitors (heart rate, blood pressure) to implanted devices (pacemakers) to emergency systems. Management must maintain privacy and protect access based on role (doctors can configure; nurses can read data only). Timely delivery of critical data is essential: alerts must reach physicians in seconds if a patient's condition changes. Security and privacy must prevent unauthorized access to sensitive health information.

Building automation controls lights, heating, ventilation, and security across 10 to 100,000 sensors in a building or campus. Networks often use mesh topologies with multi-hop communication. Managers must verify that expected devices are present, detect unwanted devices, and ensure systems respond to critical events (fire alarms, security sensors) within required timeframes. Home automation is similar but typically operated more informally, often by residents or outsourced to service providers.
sections.plainLanguage: Utilities manage millions of electric meters, often organized in self-healing mesh networks. Hospitals use body sensors to watch patients and need instant alerts if something goes wrong. Smart homes control lights and heating but also need to keep passwords and health data private. Each scenario has different requirements for speed, security, and how many devices one management system must handle.

sections.title: Transport and Field Operations
sections.content:
Transport applications include vehicles, traffic control, smart parking, and fleet management. Devices in moving vehicles connect via long-distance wireless (LTE, WiMAX) and must work even when connectivity is intermittent. Management topology is often hierarchical, with different entities managing different parts (car makers manage in-vehicle devices; public agencies manage traffic lights; service providers manage backend systems). The NMS must handle different device types and proprietary protocols while ensuring safety (incorrect traffic signal timing can cause accidents).

Community networks use constrained wireless routers (with 16 MB RAM and 200+ MHz CPUs) in mesh topologies where users install and manage them. Links are dynamic and lossy. Unlike controlled environments, community networks lack centralized configuration and must use ad hoc routing protocols. A single management station may not always reach all routers due to topology changes, so distributed monitoring and management are needed.

Field operations (rescue, security) operate mobile networks in hostile environments where equipment is heterogeneous, configurations are mostly manual, and different government agencies use incompatible standards. Networks must tolerate high failure and disconnection rates, handle multiple gateways, and support hierarchical management where local operators respond to changing conditions. The NMS must coordinate between diverse intra- and inter-governmental agencies with conflicting standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Vehicles and traffic lights must be managed across wide areas with spotty cell coverage. Volunteer community networks use cheap routers installed on rooftops, which create their own topology without central control. Emergency responders use mission-critical radios and must quickly adapt when deployed to floods or fires.
